en: The Questions of King Milinda, Chapter on Nibbāna: 1.
The Question on the Analysis of Contact and the Other [Aggregates]
The King said:
"Venerable Nāgasena, is it possible, when these mental states have come together into a single state, to separate them again and again and point out their distinction thus:
'This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness'?"
“This is applied thought, this is sustained thought.
“It is not possible, Great King, to describe the distinction between these mental states when they have reached a state of unity by repeatedly separating them out, saying:
‘This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness.’”
“This is applied thought (vitakka), this is sustained thought (vicāra).
“Give me a simile,” [the king said].
“Just as, great king, a royal cook might prepare a dish that is either flavorless or flavorful, and he might add curd to it there...”
He might add salt, he might add ginger, he might add cumin, he might add black pepper, or he might add other various ingredients;

then the king would say to him: "Bring me the flavor of the curd, bring me the flavor of the salt, bring me the flavor of the ginger, bring me the flavor of the cumin, bring me the flavor of the black pepper."
"Bring me the flavor; bring me the flavor of all those things you have put in.

Now, Great King, would it be possible to extract the flavor from those juices once they have become a single mass, separating them out again and again—the sourness, or the saltiness, or the bitterness, or the pungency, or the astringency?
"Or sweetness?

"Certainly not, venerable sir; it is not possible, having repeatedly separated those flavors once they have come together into a single state, to extract a flavor as sourness, or saltiness, or bitterness, or pungency, or astringency."
“Or sweetness; rather, they appear each with its own respective characteristic.
“In the same way, Great King, it is not possible to describe the distinction between these phenomena when they have come to a state of unity, by separating them again and again, saying:
‘This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is...’”
‘This is volition, this is consciousness, this is applied thought, this is sustained thought,’ yet they appear each with its own individual characteristic.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena!”
The first question: On the Analysis of Contact and the Other [Aggregates].
